RELIEF SOUGHT
Applicant respectfully requests that Circuit Justice Kagan issue an
injunction pending appeal under Supreme Court Rule 22 and 28 U.S.C. 1651,
ordering Respondents to cease enforcing their policy of viewpoint-based removal of
speakers from Anchorage Assembly public testimony sessions
— a policy that
continues to chill the First Amendment rights of every Anchorage citizen who
witnessed or learned of Applicant's armed removal for reciting the Pledge of
Allegiance and proclaiming religious beliefs. This injury is ongoing, continuous, and
independent of any election calendar.
Specifically, Applicant requests an order: (I) prohibiting Respondents from
removing any speaker from Assembly public testimony based on religious
expression, recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance, or any other viewpoint-based
ground; and (2) restoring Applicant's full access to Assembly public forums on a
viewpoint-neutral basis.
JURISDICTION
This Court has jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1254(1) and 28 U.S.C. 1651.
The underlying appeal is pending before the United States Court of Appeals for the
Ninth Circuit, Case No. 26-1606, arising from the March 16, 2026 order of Chief
District Judge Sharon L. Gleason, United States District Court for the District of
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden u LaFrance, No. 26-1606 — Page 3

Alaska, Case No. 3:26-cv-00053-SLG, denying Applicant's motion for a preliminary
injunction. Justice Kagan is the Circuit Justice for the Ninth Circuit.
PROCEEDINGS BELOW AND ma--1AUSTION OF LOWER COURT
REMEDIES
On February 2, 2026, Applicant filed a civil rights complaint under 42 U .S.C.
S 1983 in the District of Alaska asserting First Amendment viewpoint
discrimination, religious viewpoint discrimination, prior restraint, and related
violations arising from his removal from the Anchorage Assembly public testimony
podium on January 13, 2()26, and complete exclusion from the January 27, 2026
Assembly meeting. Case No. 3:26-cv-00053-SLG.
On March 16, 2026, Chief District Judge Gleason denied Applicant's motion
for a preliminary injunction, finding the removal was viewpoint neutral under
White v. City of Norwalk, 900 F.2d 1421 (9th Cir. 1990), and that irreparable harm
was speculative. District Court Docket 45.
On March 17, 2026, Applicant filed a Notice of Appeal and Emergency Motion to
Expedite and for Injunctive Relief Pending Appeal in the Ninth Circuit, Case No.
26-1606,
Docket Entry 3. Applicant filed a full reply brief in support of the emergency
motion. On April
8, 2026, the Ninth Circuit denied the emergency motion in a one-sentence order
signed by the Clerk. Docket Entry 8.1. The denial stated only: 'The motion (Docket
Entry No. 3) to expedite is denied. The existing briefing schedule remains in effect.'
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden v. LaFrance. NO. 26-1606 — Page 4

No merits analysis was provided. Applicant now seeks relief from Circuit Justice
Kagan.
The Ninth Circuit's automatic briefing schedule sets Applicant's opening brief due
April 14, 2026. Full merits briefing will not conclude until after May 12, 2026. The
ongoing First Amendment injury to the Anchorage public cannot wait for that
schedule. Nor can the injury await the full trajectory of ordinary appellate
proceedings. Even after merits briefing closes — with Applicant's opening brief due
April 14 and Respondents' answering brief due May 12 — a three-judge panel must
be assigned, the record reviewed, and an opinion drafted and circulated. Ninth
Circuit merits panels routinely take six months to over a year to issue a decision
after briefing is complete. If that panel decision is then challenged, a petition for
rehearing en banc under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 35 and Ninth Circuit
Rule 35-3 requires circulation to all twenty-nine active Ninth Circuit judges, a call
for a vote, and if granted, full rebriefing before the en banc court — a process that
itself routinely consumes an additional six months to two years. The total timeline
from today to a final Ninth Circuit disposition could easily extend to 2028. Every
Assembly meeting conducted under Respondents' viewpoint-discriminatory policy
between now and that date is a meeting at which religious speakers and those who
would recite the Pledge of Allegiance are deterred from participation by the
memory of armed removal of a speaker for exactly that expression.
The urgency of First Amendment relief in the public forum context is not a novel
proposition. In Marshall v. Amuso, 571 F. Supp. 3d 412 (E.D. Pa. 2021), the court
found that removal of a public commenter from a government meeting — visible to
the public audience present — was suffcient to support preliminary injunctive
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden u LaFrance, NO. 26-1606 — Page 5

relief on an expedited basis, independent of any election deadline, because the
chilling effect on future public speech constituted ongoing irreparable harm that
could not wait for ordinary merits adjudication. The Marshall court's reasoning
applies with full force here: the constitutional injury caused by a government body
using armed agents to remove a speaker for religious expression in a designated
public forum does not pause while appellate dockets clear. Justice Marshall's
foundational holding in Police Department of Chicago v. Mosley, 408 U.S. 92, 95-
96 (1972), that government restriction of expression based on viewpoint is the
highest order of First Amendment violation, compels the conclusion that relief must
be immediate. The combination of Mosley s constitutional command, Marshall v.
Amuso's recognition that public forum chilling effects are inherently emergent, and
Elrod v. Burns' categorical rule that loss of First Amendment freedoms constitutes
irreparable injury per se, 427 U.S. 347, 373 (1976), leaves no basis for concluding
that this injury can await a timeline measured in years.
STATEMENT OF FACTS
On January 13, 2026, the Anchorage Assembly held a regularly noticed
public meeting. A public comment period was opened. Applicant was invited to the
public testimony podium. During his testimony, Applicant recited the Pledge of
Allegiance and proclaimed his religious beliefs. Respondents dispatched armed
security personnel who physically removed Applicant from the podium and from
the Assembly chambers mid-testimony, in the presence of a live public audience
and on a broadcast viewable online.
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden u LaFrance, NO. 26-1606 — Page 6

Respondents' own filing in the district court — Docket 31, page 2 — states in
writing that Applicant was removed because his testimony 'included reciting the
Pledge of Allegiance and proclaiming his religious beliefs. ' This admission is
unambiguous, undisputed, and dispositive. It is the viewpoint basis for the removal
stated in Respondents' own hand.
On January 27, 2026, Respondents excluded Applicant entirely from the
subsequent Assembly meeting. He received no notice, no hearing, and no
individualized finding. He was offered only the ability to watch online and submit
a constitutionally inadequate substitute for in-person
written comments
testimony in a designated public forum.
Respondents have defended this removal policy as constitutional in every
court filing in every court. The policy is currently in force. Every Assembly meeting
conducted under this policy is a meeting at which speakers who share Applicant's
religious expression or who would recite the Pledge are deterred from participating.
That chilling effect is ongoing today.
ARGUMENT
1. THE GOVERNMENT INVITED SPEECH AND USED ARMED AGENTS
TO SUPPRESS DISFAVORED VIEWPOINT — A FIRST AMENDMENT
USURPATION THAT IS ONGOING AND INDEPENDENT OF ANY
ELECTION.
EmergencyApplication to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden u LaFrance, NO. 26-1606 — Page 7

The constitutional violation here requires no inference. The Anchorage
Assembly publicly noticed a meeting, opened a public comment period, called
Applicant to the podium, permitted him to begin testimony, and then dispatched
armed security personnel to physically remove him because his testimony included
the Pledge of Allegiance and a proclamation of religious faith. Respondents admit
this in their own court filing.
This is a government usurpation of First Amendment rights. The Assembly
created the forum, extended the invitation, waited to hear the viewpoint, and
deployed state-authorized armed force to punish it. As Justice Marshall wrote for
a unanimous Court in Police Department of Chicago v. Mosley, 408 U.S. 92, 95-96
(1972): 'above all else, the First Amendment means that government has no power
to restrict expression because of its message, its ideas, its subject matter, or its
content.' A government body cannot create a public forum, invite the public to
speak, and then use armed agents to remove speakers whose viewpoint it disfavors.
This also violates the unconstitutional conditions doctrine. The government
may not grant access to a public benefit — here the right to testifr at a publicly
noticed meeting — on condition that the speaker surrender a constitutional right.
Perry v. Sindermann, 4()8 U.S. 593, 597 (1972). The Assembly granted Applicant
podium access and then conditioned continued access on surrender of his right to
religious expression. That condition is unconstitutional on its face.
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden u LaFrance, No. 26-1606 — Page 8

11. THE PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE IS PROCEDURALLY GERMANE TO
GOW,RNMENT LEGISLATIVE MEETING — THE DISTRICT COURT'S
GERMANENESS FINDING CANNOT SURVIVE RESPONDENTS' OWN
WRITTEN ADMISSION.
The Anchorage Assembly opens its own meetings with the Pledge of
Allegiance. A speaker who recites the Pledge at an Assembly public comment period
is not departing from the subject of government business — the speaker is invoking
the same civic ritual the Assembly itself employs. The Pledge is procedurally
consonant with, not disruptive of, the Assembly's own meeting practices.
More critically, Respondents' own Docket 31 does not state that Applicant
failed to address the agenda item. It states his testimony included the Pledge and
religious expression. A germaneness determination under White v. City of Norwalk,
900 F.2d 1421, 1425 (9th Cir. 1990), requires a contemporaneous, individualized,
content-neutral finding that the speech as a whole was not germane. Respondents
made no such finding. They removed Applicant because of the viewpoint expressed.
W'7Lite does not cover viewpoint discrimination.
111. THE ONGOING PUBLIC CHILLING EFFECT ON RELIGIOUS AND-
CONSTITUTIONAL SPEECH IS INDEPENDENTLY SUFFICIENT AND
HAS NO EXPIRATION DATE.
The most important ground in this Application is the ongoing chilling effect
on the First Amendment rights of every Anchorage citizen who witnessed or
learned of Applicant's armed removal for religious expression and the Pledge of
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden u LaFrance, No. 26-1606 — Page 9

Allegiance. This ground does not depend on any election. It was not mooted by April
7. It exists today and will exist at every future Assembly meeting conducted under
Respondents' current policy.
Mosley protects not only the removed speaker but the public's right to hear
and give speech of all viewpoints in an open forum unconstrained by government
viewpoint preferences. 408 U.S. at 95-96. When the government publicly and on
broadcast television dispatches armed personnel to remove a speaker for religious
expression and the Pledge, it sends an unmistakable message to every other citizen:
bring this viewpoint to this podium and the same will happen to you. That is the
chilling effect doctrine. Rhodes v. Robinson, 408 F.3d 559, 568 (9th Cir. 2005) (test
is whether a person of ordinary firmness would be deterred).
The Ninth Circuit has confirmed that the public comment period of a
legislative assembly meeting is a designated public forum. Norse v. City of Santa
Cruz, 629 F.3d 966, 975-76 (9th Cir. 2()1()) (en banc). In a designated public forum,
viewpoint-based restrictions are presumptively unconstitutional and subject to
strict scrutiny. Rosenberger v. Rector & Visitors of Univ. of Va., 515 U.S. 819, 829
(1995). Religious viewpoint discrimination triggers strict scrutiny independently.
Church of Lukumi Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520, 533 (1993).
Respondents have never identified a compelling government interest served by
removing speakers for reciting the Pledge of Allegiance. They cannot meet strict
scrutiny.
Respondents' policy remains in force and has been defended as constitutional
in every filing before every court. The chilling effect persists. Every Assembly
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden v. LaFrance, No. 26-1606 Page IO

meeting conducted under this policy is a meeting in which religious speakers and
those who would recite the Pledge are deterred from participation. That continuous
injury requires immediate injunctive relief regardless of any election calendar.
lv. IRREPARABLE HARM IS ESTABLISHED AS A MATTER OF LAW.
Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347, 373 (1976): 'The loss of First Amendment
freedoms, for even minimal periods of time, unquestionably constitutes irreparable
injury.' This Court has never retreated from Elrod. A demonstrated First
Amendment violation establishes irreparable harm as a matter of law. The district
court's finding that harm was speculative cannot be reconciled with Elrod on this
record, where the viewpoint basis for removal is admitted in writing by
Respondents themselves.
V. LIKELIHOOD OF SUCCESS ON THE MERITS IS STRONG.
The merits question is straightforward: may a government body open a
public forum, invite testimony, and then use armed agents to remove a speaker
because his testimony included the Pledge of Allegiance and a proclamation of
religious faith? Under Mosley, Norse, Rosenberger, and Lukumi, the answer is
plainly no. Respondents' own written admission forecloses the only available
defense — viewpoint neutrality — before any inference is required. The district
court's reliance on White v. City of Norwalk was error because White addresses
content-neutral germaneness determinations, not viewpoint exclusions based on
religious expression and patriotic speech.
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan
Darden v. LaFrance, No. 26-1606 — Page 11

The unconstitutional conditions doctrine under Perry v. Sindermcnn
provides an independent ground of likely success. The January 27 total exclusion
without notice or hearing constitutes a prior restraint presumptively
unconstitutional under Southeastern Promotions, Ltd. v. Conrad, 420 U.S. 546
(1975).
Notably, Respondents failed entirely to address the FRAP 8 four-factor
standard in their Ninth Circuit opposition brief. They did not address Mosley,
Elrod, Norse, or the chilling effect doctrine. The Ninth Circuit's one-sentence denial
order contains no merits analysis.
Applicant's controlling legal arguments remain substantively unanswered in any
court.
VI. BALANCE OF EQUITIES AND PUBLIC INTEREST FAVOR
APPLICANT.
Respondents suffer no cognizable harm from an order requiring them to
maintain a viewpoint-neutral public forum. The government has no legitimate
interest in preserving an unconstitutional practice. Zepeda v. United States INS,
753 F.2d 719, 727 (9th Cir. 1983). The public interest strongly favors correction of
an ongoing viewpoint-discriminatory policy that uses armed state force to punish
religious expression in a government-created public forum.
CONCLUSION
Emergency Application to Circuit Justice Kagan — Darden v. LaFrance, No. 26-1606 — Page 12

The Anchorage Assembly publicly invited citizens to speak. When Applicant
brought the Pledge of Allegiance and his religious faith to the podium in a publicly
broadcast government meeting, Respondents sent armed men to remove him. They
then admitted in writing that was the reason. They have defended that conduct as
constitutional in every court. The First Amendment does not permit the
government to operate a public forum as an instrument of viewpoint control, using
armed force to punish expression it disfavors.
The ongoing chilling effect on the religious and constitutional speech of every
Anchorage citizen who witnessed that removal is a continuous, non-election-specific
First
Amendment injury that this Court has authority to remedy now. Under Mosley,
Elrod, Norse, Rosenberger, and Lukumi, the law is clear and controlling.
Respondents have never answered the chilling effect argument in any court. The
Ninth Circuit's denial contains no merits analysis.
Applicant respectfully requests that Circuit Justice Kagan issue an
injunction pending appeal and, if she deems it appropriate, refer this application to
the full Court.

BACKGROUND

Assembly chambers during public testimony" on January 13, 2026.4 Plaintiff
alleges that on that evening, he was "exercise[ing] his fundamental right to address
his elected representatives during the designated public comment period. "5
A video recording of the incident is posted on the Municipality of
Anchorage's YouTube page.6 The Court takes judicial notice of the recording as
the parties agree to its accuracy and authenticity, "ü]udicial notice of city council
minutes, transcript, and video recording as public records is proper," and such
recordings "can be accurately and readily determined from sources whose
accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned."7
The video shows that Plaintiff spoke at four separate times during the public
comment period on four agenda items on January 13, 2026.8 First, Plaintiff
argument was made as to any of the pending motions before the Court.

LEGAL STANDARD
Temporary Restraining Order and Preliminary Injunction
The standard for obtaining a temporary restraining order is "substantially
identical" to that for a preliminary injunction.63 In Winter v. Natural Resources
Defense Council, Inc., the United States Supreme Court held that plaintiffs seeking
preliminary injunctive relief must establish that (1 ) they are likely to succeed on the
merits; (2) they are likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of preliminary
relief; (3) the balance of equities tips in their favor; and (4) a preliminary injunction
is in the public interest" When, as here, the government is a party to the action,
the balance of equities factor and the public interest factor merge. 65 The Supreme
Court in Winter characterized "injunctive relief as an extraordinary remedy that may
only be awarded upon a clear showing that the plaintiff is entitled to such relief."66
Following Mnter, the Ninth Circuit addressed the first element—the
likelihood of success on the merits—and held that its "serious questions" approach
to preliminary injunctions was still valid "when applied as part of the four-element
Wfnter test."67 Under that approach, if a plaintiff shows "that there are 'serious
